DONATE TODAY Latvia’s president, Pontiff discuss peace September 05, 2026 President Edgars Rinkēvičs of Latvia discussed peace during a September 4 audience with Pope Leo XIV. “It was an honor to meet His Holiness Pope Leo XIV,” President Rinkēvičs said in a social media post . “I invited His Holiness to visit Latvia. We discussed peace in Ukraine, Europe, and the world.” Following the audience, Latvia’s president met with Cardinal Pietro Parolin, Secretary of State of His Holiness, and Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, Secretary for Relations with States and International Organizations. The Holy See Press Office said in a statement : During the cordial talks at the Secretariat of State, satisfaction was expressed at the good relations existing between the Holy See and the Republic of Latvia. The discussions also addressed matters of common interest at both the international and regional levels, with particular reference to the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, reaffirming the need for greater commitment on the part of the international community to promote peaceful solutions. For his part, President Rinkēvičs said : As always good to meet Secretary of State His Eminence Cardinal Pietro Parolin and Secretary for Relations with States His Excellency Archbishop Paul Gallagher. I appreciate efforts by the Holy See to bring back Russia’s abducted Ukrainian children to their families. Latvia, a Baltic nation of 1.9 million ( map ), is 83% Christian (38% Protestant, 25% Catholic, 20% Catholic). Pope Francis made an apostolic journey there in 2018. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: ‘If we’re not careful, the emergency docket can and will become an end-run around the standard review process.’ Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Pool via AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘If we’re not careful, the emergency docket can and will become an end-run around the standard review process.’ Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Pool via AFP/Getty Images US supreme court Ketanji Brown Jackson criticizes supreme court’s handling of emergency docket The justice called out her colleagues in a speech she made at the UDC school of law, hours after Trump filed his latest request Ariana Baio Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.09 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 12.11 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US supreme court justice Ketanji Brown Jackson acknowledged serious concerns about her colleagues’ handling of emergency requests, the method Donald Trump often uses to seek approval from the court. Jackson, one of the three liberal members of the supreme court, criticized the justices’ willingness to issue rulings via the “shadow docket”, saying it undermines the public’s faith in the judicial system. “There is a serious concern that the supreme court’s modern stay practices are having a disruptive and potentially corrosive effect,” Jackson told faculty and students at the University of the District of Columbia’s David A Clarke school of law on Thursday. Her comments came just hours after the Trump administration filed its latest emergency request – this time asking justices to allow officials to continue deporting immigrants to countries other than their own . The emergency docket, sometimes also referred to as the “shadow docket”, is where plaintiffs can request immediate relief from the supreme court in consequential cases. Justices can quickly grant or dismiss requests without conducting the same legal review that is typically required in merit cases or providing a lengthy explanation to the public. The Trump administration has used the method to rapidly push forward the US president’s agenda. Since returning to office in January 2025, the administration has filed more than 30 emergency requests. Many have been granted. Via emergency requests, the conservative wing of the supreme court has allowed Trump to temporarily end protections for migrants seeking asylum, eliminate transgender rights, roll back environmental protections, fire the officials in charge of independent federal agencies and more. The justices have faced criticism for their handling of emergency requests from members of Congress and the public. However, in July, justice Elena Kagan, another member of the liberal wing of the court, told Congress that she thought they were improving its handling of requests by providing some justification. Jackson pointed to that on Thursday, telling the audience that while the court “began to explain more”, it was “still not the full kind of explanation” that cases receive on the merits docket. “If we’re not careful, the emergency docket can and will become an end-run around the standard review process,” she added. As Jackson critiqued the court’s current methods, which have become more prominent under the second Trump administration, three of her colleagues dined with Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping at the White House. Chief justice John Roberts and justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett joined other officials for the state dinner to welcome Xi. https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/loc.text: Pennsylvania Suspects place skimming devices on Wawa ATMs to steal from customers, police say Police are searching for two men who they say placed skimming devices on ATMs at multiple Pennsylvania stores and stole money from customers. By Deanna Durante and David Chang • Published September 15, 2026 • Updated on September 15, 2026 at 5:14 pm BOOKMARKER NBC Universal, Inc. Police are searching for two men who they say stole from dozens of people after placing skimming devices on ATMs inside stores across Pennsylvania. NBC10’s Deanna Durante has the exclusive story. Police are searching for two men who they say placed skimming devices on ATMs at multiple Pennsylvania stores to steal money from dozens of customers. The investigation began on May 5, 2026, after police were alerted by a customer at the Wawa in Hilltown Township, Pennsylvania. The customer told police he inserted his card in the ATM. When he took it out, he spotted a small piece of a cloning device on the card. Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10. WATCH HERE Employees at the Wawa then found a camera device that was placed on the front of the ATM. The store employees then checked their ATMs multiple times over the next few days. About a week later, they found a second skimming device that had been installed on another ATM. View this post on Instagram Hilltown Township Police Detective James Towhey investigated the incidents, working with local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. Then in August, investigators were notified by employees at the Quakertown National Bank who said someone had used clone cards to withdraw money from victims’ accounts. Investigators determined the suspects were driving rental cars from New York to then target not only the Hilltown Township Wawa but also 7-Eleven and CVS stores in three other counties in Pennsylvania. Hilltown Township Police Hilltown Township Police L to R: Unidentified suspect, the skimming device, Grozea Daragiu Police eventually identified one of the suspects as Grozea Daragiu, a Romanian national. They have not yet identified the second suspect. Local Breaking news and the stories that matter to your neighborhood. weather forecast 3 hours ago Temperature roller coaster heading our way this week North Philadelphia 4 minutes ago Man charged after woman found beaten to death in North Philly home: Police At this point, Detective Towhey said the men could have targeted 50 to 100 customers of the Bucks County Wawa alone. As police continue to search for the suspects, Towhey shared important tips for customers using ATMs inside stores. “If you go to the ATM, whether you’ve been there 100 times or you’ve never been there before, when something doesn’t look right, don’t use it,” he said. “If it doesn’t look right, grab a hold of it. If you wiggle it or pull on it and it comes off, pieces aren’t supposed to come off ATMs once they’re installed. So, if pieces are coming off, I would say alert the bank wherever you are right away and don’t use the machines.” If you have any information on the two suspects, contact police. Photograph: Jeff Chiu/AP California Judge ends federal oversight of Oakland police department after 23 years Group of officers known as ‘riders’ in 2000s prompted longest arrangement of its kind in US history Abené Clayton Tue 29 Sep 2026 22.02 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 22.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google After 23 years, a district judge has released the Oakland police department (OPD) from federal oversight, marking the end of the longest arrangement of this kind in US history. In the early 2000s, a group of police officers known as the “riders” were exposed for offenses like planting evidence, falsifying reports and using excessive force against primarily young Black men. These actions led victims to file more than 100 civil lawsuits against the department. In 2003, as a part of the settlement of these cases, OPD was put on a federal court-ordered reform program. OPD was given more than 50 tasks to complete including collecting and analyzing data on racial profiling, dealing with complaints against officers more quickly and updating their community policing practices. Despite this, issues remained and the department’s reforms were put under the direct control of a federal judge in 2012. Since then, the department has still had its share of scandals including allegations that several OPD officers sex-trafficked a teenage girl; nearly a dozen officers were either fired or suspended . The investigation into the trafficking of the teenager began in 2015 and OPD issued her a nearly $1m settlement in 2017. For organizers against police misconduct and brutality, the decision to end the federal oversight scheme does not mean that the department should be free of scrutiny. “Police cannot police themselves. Oakland’s history has already taught us that lesson,” the Anti Police-Terror Project (APTP) said in a statement following the judge’s decision. “The end of federal oversight does not mean the end of police misconduct. It does not erase the history that brought OPD under federal supervision. And it certainly does not mean Oakland should simply trust OPD to hold itself accountable.” Explore more on these topics California US policing West Coast news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
